Signing Real Tokens in Integration Tests

The integration suite doesn't fake authentication out either — every protected request carries a real, valid Bearer token.

Every route this project has protected this lesson now needs a real token to reach at all — so the integration suites (mocked Prisma, real Express routing, since Lesson 2) sign real ones too, rather than mocking authenticate.js out of the picture:

// Figure 4.17: real tokens for fake users (tests/integration/tickets.routes.test.js, excerpt)
const customerToken = signToken({ sub: 13, role: 'customer' });
const agentToken = signToken({ sub: 14, role: 'agent' });
const adminToken = signToken({ sub: 99, role: 'admin' });

const asCustomer = (req) => req.set('Authorization', `Bearer ${customerToken}`);
const asAgent = (req) => req.set('Authorization', `Bearer ${agentToken}`);

Three tokens, signed once at the top of the file, cover every role this suite needs to act as — sub: 13/sub: 14 deliberately match the customerId: 13/assignedAgentId: 14 values the mocked Prisma responses use elsewhere in the same file, so a test asserting "an agent sees their own assigned ticket" is actually exercising scopeForViewer (the role- scoped-queries topic) against numbers that genuinely line up, not arbitrary ones. asCustomer(request(app).get('/tickets')) reads as "make this request as a customer" — a small helper wrapping supertest's own .set(...), used the same way sendResource/sendCollection gave every controller a shared vocabulary (Lesson 3).

Nothing about authenticate.js or authorize.js is mocked here — a real token really does need to pass real signature verification (verifyToken, this lesson's JWT topic) to reach the mocked-Prisma-backed controller underneath it, which is exactly what makes a test like "POST /tickets is forbidden for an agent" trustworthy: it's proof the actual authorize middleware rejects the request, not an assumption based on what the test expected to happen.
